text: For part of every year, a huge stretch of western India is a shallow wetland. Then the water dries up, and leaves behind something you won't find anywhere else in the country: a flat, white desert of salt, thousands of square kilometres across. And on an island in the middle of it sits a city that was planned and built about five thousand years ago. This is the Rann of Kutch. Its season has just begun, and in this video you'll see why it deserves a trip this winter.
The Rann of Kutch. India's white desert, and a five thousand year old city.

The Rann lies in Kutch district, in the far west of Gujarat. To its north is Sindh, in Pakistan, and beyond that the Thar Desert. To its south is the Kutch mainland, with the Gulf of Kutch and the Arabian Sea. The Great Rann is the big northern part. A smaller one, the Little Rann, sits to the south east.

How big is it? That depends on where you draw the edge. Wikipedia puts the Great Rann at about seven thousand five hundred square kilometres. Britannica gives a much bigger figure, about eighteen thousand square kilometres. The Little Rann adds roughly five thousand more. And almost all of it is astonishingly flat, averaging only about fifteen metres above sea level.

There's a reason it's so low and so flat. This whole area was once a shallow arm of the Arabian Sea. Over time, the land rose and the connection to the sea was cut off. Accounts say the area was still navigable in the time of Alexander the Great. What the sea left behind is a basin of salty clay and mudflats, and that is what makes the white desert possible.

Here is how it works. In the monsoon, water pours into the basin and much of the Rann becomes a wetland. In very wet years, the water can reach from the Gulf of Kutch to the Gulf of Khambhat. Then the rains stop, the sun takes over, and the water evaporates. What is left is a crust of white salt on the ground. That's the white desert visitors come to see, and it's at its best in the cool, dry months of winter. Just don't come in summer, when temperatures can climb close to fifty degrees.

The Rann is not empty, though. A huge part of it is protected as the Kutch Desert Wildlife Sanctuary, declared in nineteen eighty-six. At over seven thousand five hundred square kilometres, it is the largest sanctuary in Gujarat. Deep in its mudflats lies a place called Flamingo City. According to the Gujarat Forest Department, it is the only area in India where greater flamingos breed regularly. Nesting here was first reported back in eighteen eighty-three, and in nineteen forty-five, the ornithologist Salim Ali estimated about half a million birds at the nesting site.

Being so close to the border has given the Rann a dramatic history too. In nineteen sixty-five, India and Pakistan fought over its western end. An international tribunal settled the dispute in nineteen sixty-eight. India was awarded about ninety percent of the disputed area, and Pakistan about ten percent.

Today, the most famous way to see the white desert is the Rann Utsav, a tent city at Dhordo village, on the edge of the Great Rann. This season it runs from the first of November twenty twenty-six to the seventh of March twenty twenty-seven. Dhordo itself was named one of the U N tourism body's Best Tourism Villages in twenty twenty-three. At the craft market you'll find Kutchi work like Ajrakh block prints, Bandhani tie and dye, mirror work and Lippan art.

The best moment of all is a full moon night, when the salt glows almost silver. This season, the full moon periods fall around the twenty third to the twenty fifth of November, the twenty second to the twenty fourth of December, the twenty first to the twenty third of January, and the nineteenth to the twenty first of February. If you love stars instead, pick a dark moon night.

For the big view, head to Kalo Dungar, the Black Hill. At four hundred and sixty two metres, it's the highest point in Kutch, and from the top you look out over the salt desert. Up here is a Dattatreya temple said to be about four hundred years old. Legend says Dattatreya once offered his own body to feed starving jackals, and the priests still feed the jackals cooked rice after the evening prayers.

Now, that island in the middle of the Rann. It's called Khadir Bet, and on it lies Dholavira, one of the great cities of the Indus Valley Civilisation. UNESCO says people lived here from about three thousand to fifteen hundred B C E, and that the city flourished for nearly one and a half thousand years. Some recent research pushes its beginnings even earlier. Out of more than a thousand known Harappan sites, UNESCO ranks it the sixth largest. In July twenty twenty-one, it became a World Heritage Site.

A local man, Shambhudan Gadhvi, came across the ruins in the early nineteen sixties. The site was officially recorded in the late nineteen sixties, and then excavated over thirteen seasons, ending in two thousand and five. What they uncovered was a carefully planned city. A fortified castle at the top. A middle town. A lower town. A large open ceremonial ground. And to the west, a cemetery. The main walled city measures roughly seven hundred and seventy metres by six hundred and twenty metres.

But Dholavira's real genius was water. This is one of the driest places in India, so its people built a system to catch every drop. Two seasonal streams fed the city. Sixteen or more reservoirs were built, all in stone. Some of the big ones are about seven metres deep and close to eighty metres long. A huge stepwell found here measures about seventy three metres long and ten metres deep. It is often described as one of the earliest water conservation systems ever found.

And then there's the sign. Just outside the north gate of the citadel, archaeologists found ten large Indus script symbols, each about thirty seven centimetres tall, made of white gypsum pieces once set on a wooden board around three metres long. In July twenty twenty-six, India's Ministry of Culture called it the world's oldest known signboard. Nobody can read it, because the Indus script has never been deciphered.

Dholavira wasn't isolated, either. Workshops here made beads and jewellery from shell, agate, carnelian, copper and gold. And UNESCO notes evidence of trade with other Harappan cities, with Mesopotamia, and with Magan, the region of today's Oman peninsula.

Getting there is easier than you might think. Bhuj is the gateway, with an airport and a railway station. From Bhuj, Dhordo and the tent city are about eighty five kilometres by road, roughly an hour and a half. Dholavira is much further, about two hundred and fifty kilometres from Bhuj by the main route east. Some travellers use the Road to Heaven, a stretch of about thirty kilometres running straight across the salt flats towards Khadir. Two to three nights is a good start, with extra days for Kalo Dungar and Dholavira.

A few honest warnings before you go. Visitors to the White Rann need an entry permit, so check the latest rules and timings. It gets cold after sunset, so pack warm layers. And Diwali week, Christmas and New Year are the busiest times, so book well ahead.

So which would you go for first? The white desert under a full moon, or a five thousand year old city with the world's oldest known signboard? Tell me in the comments. And subscribe to True Scale for more places in India, drawn to true scale.
